knowledge-base.name: practices-code-review
knowledge-base.triggers: code review, pull request, PR review, CL, changelist, reviewer, author, LGTM, diff review, review comment, review feedback, review speed, small PR, small CL
knowledge-base.overview: Concrete guidance for both reviewers and authors based on Google's engineering practices. Covers what to look for, how to give and receive feedback, CL size, and speed.

what-review-is-for.purpose: Code review improves code health over time. The primary goal is to ensure every change improves the overall codebase — not to achieve perfection on each CL.

goals.goal: Correctness: does the code do what the author intends?
Maintainability: will others understand and modify this easily?
Knowledge sharing: spreads design awareness and coding practices across the team
Catches bugs, design problems, and test gaps before they reach production

not-goals.not-goal: Perfection — approve when the change improves overall code health, even if imperfect
Teaching everything you know — mark educational comments as optional
Bikeshedding style when a style guide already rules on it

item.check: Does the overall design make sense? Does this code integrate well with the rest of the system?
Should this logic be in a library instead of this service?
Does this interact correctly with other parts of the system?
Does it do what the author intended?
Are edge cases handled? What happens with null, empty, or very large inputs?
For UI changes: does this actually work? Is it accessible?
For concurrent code: are there race conditions or deadlocks?
Can each line, function, and class be understood quickly?
Is the complexity necessary, or is the author solving a problem that doesn't exist yet?
Over-engineering flag: is generic infrastructure being added for speculative future needs?
Are there appropriate unit, integration, or end-to-end tests?
Will the tests actually fail if the code breaks?
Are test assertions simple and meaningful?
Tests are code too — they have to be maintained. Are they clear?
Are names sufficiently descriptive without being verbose?
Do names communicate what something is or does?
Do comments explain WHY, not WHAT? The code shows what; comments explain why.
If a comment explains what the code does, the code should be simplified instead.
Are class and function comments accurate about purpose, usage, and behavior?
Does it follow the project style guide?
Flag optional style improvements with "Nit:" prefix so the author knows they're not blockers.
Are READMEs or guides updated to match this change?
Is documentation for deleted or deprecated code removed?

approval-standard.rule: Approve when the change demonstrably improves code health overall — even if it's not perfect.
Do not block approval because you'd have done it differently, as long as the author's approach is technically sound.
Technical facts and data override opinions. Style guides are the authority on style.
If multiple valid approaches exist and the author's choice is sound, accept their preference.
Never approve a change that would worsen overall code health.

comment-prefixes.prefix: Optional polish — author can ignore or address at their discretion

speed.target: Respond within one business day. Ideally, shortly after the request comes in if you're between tasks.

why-speed-matters.reason: Slow reviews stall features and fixes by days or weeks
Frustration with slow reviews vanishes when reviewers respond quickly, even if they request many changes
Pressure to approve substandard code builds when reviews drag on

managing-interruptions.rule: Don't interrupt focused coding work to do a review. Respond during natural breaks — after finishing a task, at lunch, between meetings.
Quick acknowledgment that a full review is coming later still helps significantly.
Responding quickly to each round matters more than completing the full process quickly.

lgtm-with-comments.use-when: The remaining comments are optional or very minor
You trust the developer will address the notes reliably
The change spans time zones and waiting another day has no benefit

large-cls.rule: Ask developers to split large changes into smaller sequential CLs.
If splitting is impossible and you lack time, provide architectural feedback rather than delaying entirely.

cl-size.target: A CL should make one minimal, self-contained change. Typically 100 lines is reasonable; 1000 is usually too large.

what-small-means.criteria: Addresses a single thing — one feature part, one bug fix, one refactoring
Keeps the system working after submission
Contains enough context for reviewers to understand it

why-small.reason: Reviewers find five-minute blocks easier than thirty-minute ones — faster turnaround
Smaller scope means more thorough review, fewer missed issues
Simpler to reason about side effects and correctness
Less wasted work if the design needs to change
Easier rollbacks when something goes wrong
Unblocks other work — you can start the next CL while this one is in review

acceptable-exceptions.exception: File deletions count as roughly one line of work
Automated refactoring from trusted tools — reviewers verify intent, not each line

splitting-strategies.strategy: Submit one small CL, start a dependent CL immediately without waiting
Separate CLs for different reviewer groups (e.g., proto changes separate from code using the proto)
Shared code or stubs in one CL, usage in another
Independent full-stack features (multiply in one CL, divide in another)
Never mix feature work and refactoring in the same CL

author-responsibilities.rule: Self-review your own diff before sending for review. Catch obvious issues yourself first.
Keep CLs small. Reviewers can reject a change solely for being too large.
Write a clear description: what this change does and why, not how.
Respond to all reviewer comments — even if just to acknowledge.
Improve the code in response to confusion, not just the review thread. Future readers won't see the review.
Add explanatory comments to code when a reviewer doesn't understand something — don't just explain in the review tool.

handling-disagreement.rule: Don't personalize feedback. Reviewer critiques are about the code, not you.
Never respond in anger — step away until you can respond professionally.
Clarify the code first. If a reviewer is confused, the code probably needs improvement.
Share context the reviewer may lack: user needs, codebase history, design rationale.
Ground disagreements in technical facts and engineering principles, not preference.
If consensus fails, escalate to team discussion or technical leads — never let a CL stall indefinitely.

writing-review-comments.rule: Be specific. "This won't handle the null case when user is unauthenticated" is useful. "This looks wrong" is not.
Explain the why behind a request, not just what to change. Reviewers often have context the author doesn't.
Ask questions to understand intent before demanding changes: "Is there a reason this uses a raw loop instead of LINQ?"
Separate blocking issues from suggestions. Use "Nit:" for suggestions so the author knows what's required vs. optional.
Review every line you're assigned. Don't skim large files — if you're too busy for a thorough review, say so and suggest a different reviewer.
Be kind. You can be direct without being harsh. Comments get written down and stay in the review history.

good-comment-patterns.pattern: Blocking: "This query will N+1 on large order lists. Eager load orders.Items here."
Nit: "Nit: 'data' is a bit vague here — 'userProfile' would be clearer."
Question: "Does this need a try/catch? What happens if the external call fails?"
FYI: "FYI: We have a shared utility for this in /shared/formatters.ts if you want to reuse it."

bad-comment-patterns.pattern: Vague: "This is wrong." — wrong how? what should it be?
Dogmatic: "This should be done with a factory." — why? is there a real benefit here?
Personal preference unmarked: "I prefer map() over forEach" (should be a Nit if anything)

cl-description.rule: The CL description should answer: what does this change do, and why?
The first line is a summary (under 72 characters): treat it like a newspaper headline.
The body explains the motivation: what problem does this solve? what was wrong before?
Reference issue/ticket numbers in the footer for traceability.
Don't describe how the code works — the diff does that. Describe why the approach was chosen if it's non-obvious.
cl-description.good-description:
Fix N+1 query loading user orders on dashboard
The orders dashboard was issuing one query per user to fetch their latest order. On a page with 50 users this produced 51 queries and caused noticeable latency (avg 2400ms, p99 8000ms).
Changed to a single JOIN query with an application-side group-by. Dashboard load time is now avg 180ms.
Fixes: #1823
cl-description.bad-description:
Fix bug
Updated the query to use a join instead of looping.

quick-reference.reviewer-must: Review every line assigned. Respond within one business day. Explain the why in comments. Approve when it improves health, not when it's perfect.
quick-reference.reviewer-must-not: Block on style when a style guide applies. Use "Nit:" only for true nitpicks. Let personal preference block a sound technical choice.
quick-reference.author-must: Self-review first. Keep CLs small and focused. Respond to all comments. Improve code, not just the review thread.
quick-reference.author-must-not: Respond in anger. Ignore comments. Combine refactoring with feature work in one CL.
